title: Why Opus 5 Feels Harder to Work With Than Previous AI Models
summary: The author argues that while Anthropic's Opus 5 AI model outperforms its predecessors (Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8) and rivals Fable in benchmarks, it feels worse to work with in practice. The issue stems from Opus 5 making bold assumptions in ambiguous situations rather than seeking clarification, unlike earlier models that paused to ask questions. The author speculates this behavior is driven by two factors: the push for self-improving AI systems and the pressure to excel in benchmarks, which favor models that make confident (but not always contextually appropriate) decisions. This creates a mismatch between benchmark performance and real-world usability, where ambiguity and nuanced decision-making are critical.
key_points: Opus 5 is more capable in benchmarks but feels worse to work with compared to Opus 4.7/4.8 and Fable.
Earlier models (e.g., Opus 4.7/4.8) asked for clarification when intent was unclear, while Opus 5 makes assumptions without checking.
Benchmark-driven training favors models that make bold, usually-correct assumptions in ambiguous scenarios.
Real-world coding tasks often involve ambiguity, where pausing to ask questions is more valuable than guessing.
The push for self-improving AI and benchmark performance may inadvertently reduce usability in practical applications.
The author prefers models that prioritize seeking clarification over making unchecked assumptions, even if it means lower benchmark scores.
